description: Computer Science students from the Universidade de São Paulo
summary:
Baymin is a distributed health support system that works far from Earth. It helps astronauts check on their own health, work through symptoms step by step, and warn the crew medical officer and the flight surgeon on Earth what happened, even when the connection to Earth is slow or down.

The system unites 3 different applications, for astronauts, crew medical officers and flight surgeons. Health data and other relevant indicators (such as the CO2 concentration on a base) flow from the astronaut application, wearables and other sensors up to a base server and then to an Earth server. When a connection can be established, medical advice can also flow down through the same system.

For emergencies that cannot wait for a reply from Earth, the Baymin application serves as a clinical decision support system. It uses decision graphs to store medical knowledge on the crew's applications so they can navigate emergencies with verified medical advice.
details:
Baymin: Mission Health Companion

What it does and how it works

Baymin is a health-support system for astronauts on long missions, where an instant answer from Earth isn't possible. Astronauts get a mobile app with daily check-ins, a health history, and a guided symptom flow. They answer simple "yes"/"no"/"not sure" questions and are told what to do now or when to contact the crew medical officer. A structured report is built automatically and sent, in parallel, to the medical officer and the flight surgeon on Earth. If the link is down, it is queued and delivered when the connection returns.

A base server reads wearable data (like heart rate) together with cabin sensors (like CO₂). For example, it flags a high heart rate that coincides with elevated CO₂, so symptoms aren't judged in isolation from the air the crew is breathing.

Benefits

  • Reliable first response guidance with clear steps, even when offline
  • The ground stays informed without anyone describing events from memory over a slow link
  • Earlier warning when an astronaut's health data deviates from their baseline level.
  • One shared health history for the astronaut, crew medical officer and flight surgeon
  • Mental health is a priority. The app encourages astronauts to make daily contributions to a journal and the daily check-in measures perceived emotional state and mental readiness.

Intended impact

We want to give crews decision support they can use on their own, with Earth as a partner and not a strict necessity. In the case of emergencies, a 40 min delay for getting medical advice might lead to the worst possible outcome; we tackle this by storing medical advice as graphs the crew can traverse with simple "yes"/"no"/"not sure" questions. We also aim to show how delay-tolerant, offline-first health tools should behave on longer space missions.

What we built and tools used

Our demo simulates a fictional Mars mission (Artemis X) with four connected screens: astronaut, medical officer, flight surgeon, and base station. The wearable and environmental sensors are simulated through a control panel. Three draft symptom flows (palpitations, urine changes, allergic reaction) are included, along with a remedy inventory running on a real FastAPI service.

Tools: TypeScript, Python, React, React Router, Vite, Tailwind CSS, FastAPI, and browser APIs (MediaRecorder, localStorage). No special hardware is needed for the demo. The full system would use wearables such as an Apple Watch, cabin and rover sensors, and crew phones.

Creativity

The largest challenge we tackled was coming up with a way to help crews navigate medical emergencies. We solved that with an innovative approach to storing and displaying medical advice so the UX can be simple and the proposed treatment is reliable and transparent.

The medical flows on our symptom guide are simply formatted data that define a graph. Each flow is a reviewable graph with a version, sources and a review status, so new space-specific conditions can be added without changing the app.

A validator guarantees every question handles "not sure" safely and that flows have no dead ends. In the proposed system, AI is limited to understanding language (matching free text or voice to a flow). It never decides treatment, keeping the system explainable and free of invented medical advice.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility under pressure: Large touch targets, and color is always paired with shape and text.
  • Integration: when connection is possible, health data flows from the crew's wearables/applications to the base server, and then Earth. Medical advice flows from Earth to the base server, and then to the crew's applications.
  • Connectivity: everything is designed to work offline
  • Honesty: we clearly separate what is built from what is simulated or proposed
